extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American state government, public administration, and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality, structure, and functioning of U.S. state judiciaries and state fiscal systems, covering selection and tenure of judges, judicial independence, salaries, and the design and administration of state taxation and revenue. The guidance is historic/descriptive but normative—identifying what helps or harms judicial quality and equitable revenue collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of judicial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Who chooses judges — legislature, governor (with confirmation), or popular election — and the historical shift toward popular elections in many States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes varieties (legislative election, gubernatorial appointment with confirmation, popular election) and the historical trend (1812–1860 and later) of vesting choice in the people. It argues popular elections place selection in hands of political parties and 'wirepullers', increasing the risk of partisan or corrupt nominations and lowering judicial character; gives state examples (New York, Mississippi, Delaware, Georgia) and explains regional patterns (older states less democratic, western/new states more so).

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular elections, short terms, and small salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The combined presence of popular elections, short judicial terms, and low salaries undermines the character and independence of the judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text asserts any one of these phenomena would lower judicial quality but their combined effect is particularly harmful: elections invite party influence; short terms induce judges to curry favor with those who put them in office; small salaries deter able lawyers from accepting the bench. Examples and salary ranges are provided to illustrate impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of tenure / life tenure vs term appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether judges hold office for life (or during good behaviour) or for fixed terms — and the implications for independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically many judges held life tenure (removable only by impeachment or legislative address). Only a few States retained life tenure; most adopted fixed terms ranging from 2 to 21 years (8–10 typical). Life tenure is praised as protecting against capricious removal; short terms are criticised for 'sapping the conscience' and discouraging independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial salaries and ability to attract talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of pay for state judges influences ability to attract competent, learned jurists and hence the bench's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides concrete salary figures ($2,500 in Vermont to $17,500 in one New York district; average $5,000–$6,000). Low salaries in many Western States and in inferior courts are singled out as a major reason able men decline the bench, producing a bench 'inferior' to practicing advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections against removal (impeachment and address)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural safeguards for judges' removal — impeachment or legislative 'address' requiring high legislative majorities — as protections of judicial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes 'good behaviour' removal standard and that removal by address usually requires a two-thirds majority in each house. This British-derived provision is called 'salutary' for preventing capricious removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political party influence and corruption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which party bosses and 'wirepullers' influence judicial selection and conduct, including participation in election fraud and use of injunctions as political moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text documents instances where judges became 'accomplices in election frauds' or 'tools in the hands of unscrupulous bosses' (Tweed Ring example). Political selection creates opportunities for reward-seeking and partisan use of judicial powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual and social parity of the bench with the bar
rubrics_metrics.description: Bench should be at least intellectually and socially on a level with the practicing bar to ensure competent decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that even absent dishonesty, a bench that is intellectually/socially inferior to the bar undermines confidence and effectiveness; the bench should not be 'below the bar' in learning or ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity, published reasons, and press scrutiny as checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency—requirements that judgments be reasoned and are reportable—serve as public checks on judicial misconduct or incapacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic theory partly cures evils of elective systems by subjecting judges to publicity: 'Whatever passes in court is, or may be, reported. The judge must give his reasons for every judgment he delivers.' A free press and public opinion make dishonourable nominations risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of the bar in nominations and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional bar's role in preventing bad nominations and in promoting competent candidates for judicial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bar often interposes against bad party nominations and can persuade parties to nominate competent members; examples given where lawyers persuaded parties to choose better candidates. The bar's professional interest in competent courts is emphasized as a corrective to partisan influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal tribunals as a corrective influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of Federal courts and capable federal judges helps maintain standards by providing a countervailing model and embarrassing poor state appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-existence of Federal tribunals, 'presided over by judges who are usually capable and almost always upright', helps keep state judges from losing dignity and makes parties ashamed to nominate clearly unfit persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall and popular reversal provisions reduce judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional provisions for recall of judges or for popular reversal of particular state-court decisions diminish judicial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes introduction of recall in Oregon, California, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and Colorado's unique power allowing the people to reverse a particular decision; warns the tendency is to reduce independence and the only serious argument for recall is presence of judges 'fit for nothing but to be recalled.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes for which State revenue is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief categories of state spending that justify raising revenue: officials' salaries and judicial incidental expenses, militia, public/charitable institutions, school grants, state prisons, state buildings/public works, and interest on state debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a numbered list of seven principal state expenses and notes that state budgets are small relative to population/wealth because local subdivisions (counties, cities, townships) bear much administrative burden. Examples of state revenue totals (New York, Massachusetts) are given for scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of taxation (state reliance on direct taxation)
rubrics_metrics.description: States rely almost wholly on direct taxation—chiefly property tax—whereas the National government raises revenue by indirect taxation (customs and excise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains constitutional limits (states cannot levy import/export duties without Congress) and that property tax on real and personal property is the dominant state revenue source. Mentions historical context (Federal income tax and 16th Amendment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation and assessment methods (assessors, appraisers, equalization boards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Property taxation depends on valuations made by assessors/appraisers under state laws; boards of equalization at state and county levels compare and revise local valuations to promote fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes assessors' duties, their appointment by local communities, the incentive to undervalue (to reduce local tax burden), and the state's response of creating equalization boards. Also notes these boards often fail to secure truly equal valuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequalities and deliberate undervaluation in assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation in assessment scales among towns leads to inequalities; assessors commonly value property below actual worth causing unfair tax distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Connecticut examples where market price is basis but real estate valued at one-third to three-fourths, plus evidence of marked differences in household furniture listings between neighboring towns. Political pressure can penalize assessors who insist on accurate valuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intangible property escapes taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: A large part of wealthy individuals' property is intangible (notes, bonds, book debts, mortgages) and is practically impossible to tax effectively because it is not easily discoverable except by owner declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission reports (Connecticut, West Virginia, Baltimore) show dramatic declines in intangible property on tax lists; owner oaths and voluntary disclosure are ineffective; result is that only conscientious citizens, widows, executors bear taxes on this property while many evade it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of collection and enforcement (oaths ineffective, political costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on sworn declarations and weak enforcement undermines tax collection; assessors who pursue hidden property risk political backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text records that oaths refer only to 'best knowledge, remembrance, or belief' and perjury has become common; auditors/assessors who force disclosure risk electoral defeat (example of assessor who added $200,000 and then lost election).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probate records and comparative audits to detect escaped property
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing tax returns with probate inventories reveals large amounts of personal property escaping taxation and can be used as evidence of underassessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connecticut commissioners found probate records and last tax returns had 'few points of contact', concluding a large proportion of personal property escaped taxation; similar findings reported in other states and used to recommend reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board of Equalization and commissions as reform tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of state or county equalization boards and special tax commissions is a common remedy recommended to correct local undervaluation and tax inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards compare and revise valuations across localities; special commissions (e.g., Connecticut tax commission, New York special tax commissioner) produce reports recommending reforms such as alternative bases for taxation (some commissions propose taxing real estate only) and draw attention to systemic failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and legal limitations on state taxing power
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal constraints (e.g., Federal Constitution's restriction on state import/export duties) limit forms of taxation states may impose and shape state revenue choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the Federal Constitution forbids states levying import/export duties except with Congress's consent and directs any such duties to Federal treasury; this compels states toward direct taxes on property as chief revenue source.
